title: Webb finds brown dwarfs only about twice Jupiter's mass
freshness: NASA's IC 348 page lists a last update of 21 September 2026, within the 15-day freshness window.
excerpt: In the star-forming region IC 348, about 1,000 light-years away in Perseus, Webb has found brown dwarfs with masses down to about twice Jupiter's, or 0.19 percent of the Sun's mass. They are the least massive brown dwarfs known, lighter than star-formation models predicted, and one of the lightest shows signs of a disk.
whyItMatters: The smallest stars weigh about 8 percent of the Sun. These objects formed by cloud collapse, like stars, yet sit near two Jupiter masses. That pushes the bottom of star formation below where the models had placed it, and it blurs any rule that tries to separate brown dwarfs from giant planets by mass alone.

exploreFurther.label: NASA Science: Webb Reveals Dynamic Panorama of Star Formation

whatToExploreNext: How astronomers tell a brown dwarf born from a cloud from a giant planet born in a disk, when the masses overlap.
body:
## Below the mass the models expected

IC 348 is a star-forming region about 1,000 light-years away, in the constellation Perseus. Cold clouds of molecular hydrogen collapse there and build new stars. The view Webb just released is one of the largest images the telescope has put out to the public. Astronomers used it to search for brown dwarfs, and they found objects down to about twice the mass of Jupiter.

A brown dwarf forms the way a star does, through the collapse of a molecular cloud, but its core never gets hot enough to fuse ordinary hydrogen into helium. Many brown dwarfs briefly fuse deuterium, a heavy form of hydrogen, early in their lives. The smallest true stars weigh about 8 percent of the Sun's mass. Below that line the object is a brown dwarf, even though the birth recipe was the same collapse that makes stars.

Twice Jupiter's mass is about 0.19 percent of the Sun's mass. NASA and ESA both call these the least massive brown dwarfs known, far smaller than theory predicted, and a challenge to models of how stars form. The data come from Webb General Observer Program 4866. ESA names the principal investigators as K. Luhman and C. Alves de Oliveira. NASA's image credit lists Kevin Luhman (PSU), Catarina Alves de Oliveira (ESA), and Mahdi Zamani (ESA/Webb). These releases identify program leadership and image credit, not a journal author list.

## From a wide image to a spectrum

The same team pointed Webb at IC 348 in 2022 and found brown dwarfs as light as three to four times Jupiter's mass. This pass goes lower. In 2024 they used NIRCam, Webb's Near-Infrared Camera, to catch the warm glow of young brown dwarfs and newborn stars in the new image. Candidates were selected from color and brightness. In 2025 they followed up with NIRSpec, the Near-Infrared Spectrograph, and used those spectra to study the masses.

Color and brightness only select a candidate. The mass comes from the later spectra. The releases state the floor and do not print an uncertainty beside it, so "twice Jupiter" is the precision they are willing to give.

The question taken to IC 348 was the bottom of star formation: how small an object can a collapsing cloud still make? The 2022 floor sat at a few Jupiter masses. The later spectra move the known floor to about two. That conflicts with the models the releases cite. It does not replace them. NASA and ESA state the challenge and do not say which piece of the theory has to move.

## A disk, a hydrocarbon, and maybe a class of their own

One of the lightest new brown dwarfs shows signs of a disk. NASA reads that as a hint that small planets could be forming around an object that itself has only about a planet's mass. ESA says planets could be forming around it even though the brown dwarf weighs about as much as a planet. The disk is the reported sign. Planets inside it are a suggestion, not a detection of a second object.

In the spectra, the team found a feature they attribute to a hydrocarbon, a molecule built only from hydrogen and carbon. NASA calls the carrier an unidentified hydrocarbon. The feature has been seen only in the atmospheres of the lowest-mass brown dwarfs, and the team suggests these objects might belong to a spectral class of their own. That is an inference from where the feature shows up, not a chemical identification with a lab match. A repeated bump can mean a shared atmosphere. It can also mean a shared temperature and haze.

Program 4866 has two further aims beyond the mass floor. One is to compare populations of planetary-mass objects between star-forming regions, and to see whether IC 348's tiny brown dwarfs are typical or local. The other is to chase the origin of the hydrocarbon feature in the lowest-mass objects. Both are questions the program is built to ask. Neither is answered by the image release alone.

## Jets in the same cloud, and a boundary drawn by mass

The upper right holds protostars still gathering mass. Several drive jets into nearby gas and dust, lighting Herbig-Haro objects, the glowing shocks those collisions make. HH 797, previously a Webb Picture of the Month, is two protostars with nearly parallel outflows. HH 211, just beside it, shows narrow jets and broader outflows in a propeller shape. A collage also marks the central cluster, fainter flows, gravitational lensing, and background spiral galaxies.

The cloud is still building ordinary stars, complete with outflows, while the census at the bottom has gone below the mass where the models were comfortable. Star formation here runs from massive stars that will explode in a few million years down to brown dwarfs of about two Jupiter masses.

Mass alone no longer sorts the recipes. A free-floating object of two Jupiter masses in a star-forming cloud can be a brown dwarf, born from collapse, with no star required. A planet grows inside a disk around a star. Jupiter shows that a disk can build something huge. These brown dwarfs show the other direction: cloud collapse did not stop where the models were comfortable. An isolated object with only a mass on the label inherits the ambiguity. Birthplace is what sorts them.

The releases do not say Jupiter formed by collapse, and they do not claim confirmed planets around these brown dwarfs. One of the lightest has signs of a disk. NASA's page and ESA's note weic2619 are the accounts to read before quoting the mass any more tightly than the agencies do.
